nameStory: The walleye gets its distinctive name from its large, glassy eyes that seem to stare outward with a somewhat vacant expression. These marble-like eyes have a reflective quality that makes them appear almost wall-eyed or cross-eyed, especially when light hits them at certain angles.
description: The walleye is a sleek, golden-bronze freshwater fish with distinctively large, glassy eyes that give it an almost hypnotic stare. This popular game fish typically grows 12-20 inches long and has a streamlined body built for swift swimming in lakes and rivers. Its olive-green to golden-yellow coloration and white-tipped fins make it one of the more beautiful members of the perch family.

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Large, marble-like eyes with a glassy, reflective quality that appear cloudy or milky white when light hits them - they feel smooth and cool to touch

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Golden-bronze to olive-green body with a brassy sheen that feels smooth and slightly slimy; darker vertical bars may be visible along the sides

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Two separate dorsal fins with the front one spiny and rigid to touch; tail and lower fins have distinctive white tips that stand out against darker fin membranes

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Streamlined, torpedo-shaped body that tapers smoothly from head to tail; feels firm and muscular with smooth, small scales

idTips.label: Mouth
idTips.description: Large mouth extending to about the middle of the eye with sharp teeth that feel like tiny needles - handle with care

habitat: Walleyes prefer the cooler, deeper waters of New England's larger lakes and river systems, particularly in northern Vermont, New Hampshire, and Maine. They thrive in clear to slightly murky waters with rocky or sandy bottoms, often near drop-offs, points, and submerged structures where they can ambush prey.

seasonality.spring: Spawning season brings walleyes into shallow, rocky areas where they're more easily spotted. Males develop a rougher texture and may show slightly more vibrant coloration during this time.
seasonality.summer: Fish move to deeper, cooler waters during the day but may venture into shallows at dawn and dusk. Their golden coloration is most pronounced in summer sunlight.
seasonality.fall: Walleyes begin feeding heavily and may be found in various depths. Their eyes appear especially glassy and prominent as water temperatures cool.
seasonality.winter: Fish remain active under ice in deeper waters, though they move more slowly and their colors may appear more muted in the dim winter light.

funFact: Walleyes have a special reflective layer behind their retinas called the tapetum lucidum - the same feature that makes cats' eyes glow in the dark - which helps them hunt in murky water and low light conditions where other fish can't see.
confusionNotes: Often confused with yellow perch, but walleyes are much larger with that distinctive glassy-eyed stare, while yellow perch have smaller, clearer eyes and more defined vertical stripes. Memory trick: 'Wall-eye' has that vacant, staring look, while perch eyes look alert and focused.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'walleyed pike' or 'yellow pike' in some regions, walleyes are not related to true pikes at all - they're actually members of the perch family. This naming confusion has persisted for generations and can mislead anglers about the fish's behavior and habitat preferences.
compareHints: As the only member of the pikeperch genus in New England, walleyes are most similar to their perch family cousins like yellow perch, but are much larger and lack the perch's distinct vertical stripes. Unlike the smaller darters in their family, walleyes have that signature large, reflective eye and streamlined body built for open water rather than bottom-dwelling.
